plan.contextChunk: This figure pairs two panels side by side to tie the circular and graphical pictures of the sine function together. At the left, drawn faintly in gray, is a unit circle crossed by its axes and by a fan of radii at the special angles. At the right is a Cartesian plot with a horizontal axis labeled x and a vertical axis labeled y ticked at 1, 0, and -1; a solid dark blue curve labeled y = sin(x) enters from the left with an arrowhead, passes through the origin, climbs to a peak of 1, and turns downward toward a second arrowhead. Four dashed orange vertical segments drop from the curve to x-axis ticks labeled pi/6, pi/4, pi/3, and pi/2, and four dashed teal horizontal lines run leftward from those same curve points, across the gap between panels, to matching heights on the gray circle. The teal connectors carry the comparison the figure is built for: the height of a point on the unit circle at a given angle is the value plotted above that angle on the graph. Reading the sine graph as a running record of height on the circle is what lets quadrant position account for the sign of the function.

interactionPlan.concept: The graph of y = sin(x) is a running record of the vertical height (y-coordinate) of a point traveling around the unit circle, so the value plotted above any angle x equals that circle point's height, and the quadrant fixes the sign.
elements: left panel: faint gray unit circle centered on its own origin
left panel: gray horizontal and vertical axes through the circle center
left panel: fan of faint gray radii at the special angles (every 30°/45°)
right panel: horizontal x-axis with arrowheads at both ends, labeled x
right panel: vertical y-axis with arrowheads, labeled y, ticked at 1, 0, -1
right panel: solid dark-blue sine curve labeled y = sin(x), entering from the left with an arrowhead, passing through the origin, peaking at 1 near pi/2, then descending toward a second arrowhead
four dashed orange vertical segments dropping from the curve to x-axis ticks labeled pi/6, pi/4, pi/3, pi/2
four dashed teal horizontal lines running leftward from those curve points across the gap to the matching heights on the gray circle
dynamic highlighted radius on the unit circle at the current angle (colored, e.g. red)
dynamic point marker on the unit circle at the current angle
dynamic point marker on the sine curve at the current x
dynamic dashed teal horizontal connector joining the circle point's height to the curve point
dynamic dashed orange vertical from the curve point to the x-axis at the current x

interactions.label: Angle x (radians)
interactions.teaches: Dragging the angle moves the radius and the circle point, and the matching point on y = sin(x) slides to the same height at the same time — the live teal connector stays perfectly horizontal, proving the graph's value at x is exactly the circle point's y-coordinate.

interactions.label: Sweep 0 to pi/2
interactions.teaches: As the radius rotates from 0 to pi/2, the sine curve is traced from the origin up to its peak, making the graph read as a continuous running record of the circle point's vertical height rather than an abstract formula.

demo_steps.title: Circle and graph side by side
demo_steps.narration: The four teal dashed lines link each special-angle point on the unit circle to the point on y = sin(x) at the same height, showing that the graph's value above an angle equals the circle point's vertical coordinate.

demo_steps.title: Watch the running record
demo_steps.narration: The radius sweeps from 0 to pi/2 while the blue curve is drawn from the origin to its peak of 1 — the graph is literally the circle point's height recorded as the angle increases.

demo_steps.title: Pin any angle
demo_steps.narration: Drag the slider to an arbitrary angle: the circle point, the horizontal teal connector, and the curve point all move together, and the connector stays level, confirming sine is the height at every angle, not just the labeled ones.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: sin(x) is nothing more than the y-coordinate (height) of the unit-circle point at angle x, so the sine graph is just that height plotted against the angle — which is why the quadrant of the circle point determines the sign of the function.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two coordinated panels separated by a gap. Left: a faint light-gray unit circle with gray cross axes and a fan of thin gray radii at the special angles; keep it deliberately low-contrast so it reads as the 'source' picture. Right: black x and y axes with arrowheads, y ticked and labeled 1, 0, -1, x labeled at the right; a thick dark-blue sine curve with arrowheads at both ends and an italic blue label y = sin(x) near the peak. Four dashed orange verticals at pi/6, pi/4, pi/3, pi/2 with pi-fraction tick labels under the x-axis, and four dashed teal horizontals from those curve points leftward to the same heights on the gray circle. Overlay a single highlighted (e.g. red) radius plus a dot on the circle and a dot on the curve, joined by a live dashed teal horizontal line and a live dashed orange vertical, all driven by the slider; during the animation these sweep from angle 0 to pi/2 tracing the curve. The horizontal teal connector staying level while both endpoints move is the visual proof to emphasize.

authoredContext:
Notice how the sine values are positive between 0 and π, which correspond to the values of the sine function in quadrants I and II on the unit circle, and the sine values are negative between π and 2π, which correspond to the values of the sine function in quadrants III and IV on the unit circle. See the figure.

Plotting values of the sine function

A side-by-side graph of a unit circle and a graph of sin(x). The two graphs show the equivalence of the coordinates.

Now let’s take a similar look at the cosine function. Again, we can create a table of values and use them to sketch a graph. The table lists some of the values for the cosine function on a unit circle.
